summary: Percé's Cap Blanc light: a wooden tower lit in 1874, replaced in 1915 by a concrete tower, kept by three Bourget generations; the end of the light is disputed.

structures.note: Height disputed: 20 ft in the 1874 report as quoted by the magazine and LighthouseFriends; about 8.9 m (29 ft) in the Quebec register. Base survives on private land.

38 ft (11.6 m) per the register and the magazine; white with red lantern. LighthouseFriends gives 24 ft (7.3 m) and names Joseph-Octave Boucher as builder (magazine and register: Joseph Antoine Boucher / Joseph Boucher). Standing.

access.note: Grounds and tower closed; surrounded by private land posted No Trespassing (LighthouseFriends).

corrections.proposed: 1915 replaced (wooden tower replaced by a reinforced-concrete tower; the light was not deactivated)
corrections.why: The 1915 date marks the replacement of the 1874 tower by a new tower lit the same year, not the end of the light. The magazine and the register both describe the new tower as lit.
The sources disagree about the end of the light (1956, 1965 automation, 1997). 1915 is the year of replacement, not deactivation. Left unset until a reviewer chooses.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register and the Les amis des phares page say the light has not worked since 1956; the magazine gives automation in 1965 and the end of the light in 1997. The register's own keeper dates run to 1965. The sources are not reconciled; the story states all three.
The 1874 report, as quoted by the magazine and LighthouseFriends, gives 20 feet (6.1 m); the register gives about 8.9 m (29 ft). Both are stated in the story.

The register gives $4,483.20 for the tower, its lighting and the inspection together. LighthouseFriends gives $1,845 for the tower and $555 for the lighting and inspection (about $2,400). The story gives both.
The magazine gives $1,429.47; LighthouseFriends gives $1,429.27. The story gives both.
The register and the magazine give 38 ft (11.6 m); LighthouseFriends gives 24 ft (7.3 m). The story states both.

The magazine names Joseph Antoine Boucher, son of the builder of the first tower; the register names Joseph Boucher de Percé; LighthouseFriends names Joseph-Octave Boucher. The story states the magazine's name and LighthouseFriends' difference.

The 1909 table names Florian Bourget with 18 March 1893 (matched by position). The 1915 table gives the same date under the initial 'P.' The 1893 date fits the start of Florian's service the magazine gives.

notes_for_editor: The magazine is copyrighted: the story paraphrases it and uses no quotations beyond short French phrases in evidence; English renderings are ours. The 1874 report figures (138 ft, 20 ft, 13 miles) come only through the magazine and LighthouseFriends; the Department's 1874 report is not in the local corpus. Florian Bourget's 1893 appointment: the 1909 table (scan p. 174, printed p. 167) prints 'Florian Bourget. Mar. 18, 1893' at a row whose station is not on the OCR line; Percé is matched by position between John Loisel (Paspebiac) and Placide Vigneau (Perroquet Island), the order the 1908 list also follows. The 1915 table (scan p. 82) prints '*Perce P'. Bourget Mar. 18, 1893' (salary 260), whose initial is read as P. (the 1912 list reads F. Bourget at Percé; E. Bourget, appointed 26 April 1910, is at Perce wharf, a different light). Neither table was checked in pixels; the 1909 row is the stronger match. The magazine says Florian died in 1919 while its own table ends his service in 1918; not reconciled. The 15-mile range is given without a unit type; the story gives it as miles and does not claim nautical miles. The 1915 tower's characteristic (flashing white every 5 s) is from the magazine and LighthouseFriends. The 1915 cost ($4,483.20) is given by both the register and the magazine; LighthouseFriends gives $1,845 + $555. The keeper of 1919 (C. T. Bourget) is named as the magazine names him. Joseph Antoine Boucher's private property is not named. Léon Bourget (keeper to 1965): the register's residence line and the magazine's 29-year line are printed in the sources and are kept; the magazine's acknowledged family contact is not named. The register's phrase 'abri du criard à brume' (and the magazine's 'abri de criard de brume') is read as a fog-signal shelter; 'criard' is unusual and the reading is ours. No storms, wrecks or rescues were found for this station.
